newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF says may conduct hearing on Nomura case.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF says may conduct hearing on Nomura case.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) is likely to ask Nomura Securities Co Ltd to explain deals done between two of its directors and a corporate client, a MOF official said on Friday.
"As the supervisor of the securities industry, the ministry will likely ask Nomura officials to explain the incident," the official said.
However, the authority to take any legal action lies in the hands of the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), which is now conducting an investigation, the official said.

"If the investigation reveals that Nomura has violated laws, the commission may urge the finance minister to take some kind of action. At that point, we will start considering whether to take punitive measures or not," he said.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference earlier on Friday that the ministry would take the necessary strict measures after seeing the results of the investigation now being made by the securities watchdog.
On Thursday, Nomura vice president Atsushi Saito publicly admitted that it was highly possible that two of its directors had been involved in illegal deals.

The Nihon Keizai Shimbun financial daily reported in its Friday evening edition that if the investigation were to show the company's involvement, the ministry would take punitive steps that would be much harsher than the ones it had imposed on the broker for past infractions.
In 1991, the securities company was found to have compensated favoured clients for losses and that its affiliates had dealings with organised crime.

At that time, the ministry suspended stock trading at Nomura's head office and its branches for four to six weeks for recommending purchases of shares in a particular company. Nomura was told that its corporate department should voluntarily refrain from conducting business for a week for compensating favoured clients, it said.
